description: Seven kinds of wave, what they're used for and what they can damage.
content_html:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic (EM) spectrum is a continuous family of transverse waves. All EM waves share three essential properties: they transfer energy, they can travel through a vacuum (they do not need a medium), and they all travel at the same speed in a vacuum — the speed of light, which is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Because speed is constant, waves with shorter wavelength have higher frequency, and vice versa.

The spectrum is arranged in order of increasing frequency (or decreasing wavelength). A useful mnemonic for the order is: Running Men In Vests Usually X-ray Giraffes — radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

Key Fact

All EM waves: travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, are transverse, carry energy, need no medium. Order (lowest to highest frequency): radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma.

Uses of Each EM Wave Type

Each region of the spectrum is suited to different applications because of its wavelength and energy. The properties that make a wave useful are the same properties that can make it dangerous if misused or overexposed.

Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies. They are used for AM and FM radio broadcasting, television signals, and some forms of long-range communication. Long-wavelength radio waves can diffract over hills and buildings, enabling reception in shadowed areas. Radio waves are generally considered non-harmful at typical exposure levels.

Microwaves are shorter than radio waves and are used in satellite communication, mobile phone networks, Wi-Fi, and microwave ovens. In ovens, microwaves cause water molecules in food to vibrate, producing internal heating. At the power levels used in communication devices, microwaves are considered non-ionising and low risk, though exposure to very intense microwave beams can heat body tissue.

Infrared radiation is emitted by all objects above absolute zero. It is used in remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, night-vision equipment, and optical fibre communications. Overexposure causes skin burns and can damage retinal tissue in the eye.

Visible light is the only part of the EM spectrum that human eyes can detect. It is used in photography, fibre optic cables, and vision itself. Lasers (a form of focused visible light) are used in surgery, engineering measurements, and barcode scanners. Very intense light (such as looking directly at a laser or the sun) can damage the retina.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation causes skin tanning, sunburn, and — with repeated overexposure — increases the risk of skin cancer by damaging DNA in skin cells. UV is used in fluorescent lamps, detecting forged banknotes (security ink fluoresces under UV), and sterilising medical equipment. The ozone layer in the atmosphere absorbs much of the UV from the Sun.

X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and metal. This makes them invaluable in medical imaging — an X-ray photograph shows bones and dense structures clearly. They are also used in airport security scanners to examine luggage. X-rays are ionising radiation: they can remove electrons from atoms, damaging DNA and potentially causing mutations or cancer. Medical staff and security workers take precautions (lead shielding, limiting exposure time) to keep doses to a minimum. This principle is known as ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable.

Gamma rays have the highest frequency and the greatest energy of all EM waves. They are emitted by radioactive nuclei. Because they are highly penetrating and ionising, they are used to treat cancer (radiotherapy targets tumours) and to sterilise medical instruments. They can also cause serious cell damage and cancer if exposure is uncontrolled. Strict safety protocols govern all medical and industrial use of gamma sources.

Ionising vs Non-Ionising Radiation

A critical distinction in radiation safety is between ionising radiation and non-ionising radiation. Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays) has sufficient energy to knock electrons out of atoms, creating charged ions. These ions can damage DNA, potentially leading to cell mutations and cancer. Non-ionising radiation (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light) does not ionise atoms, so is generally lower risk, though intense beams of any type can still cause harm through heating.

Key Fact

Ionising (can damage DNA): UV, X-rays, gamma rays. Non-ionising (lower risk): radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light. Danger generally increases with frequency because higher-frequency waves carry more energy per photon.

Risk, Benefit and the ALARA Principle

Every medical use of ionising radiation involves a risk-benefit decision. The risk of DNA damage from a single chest X-ray is very small — far less than the risk of missing an undiagnosed lung condition. A radiotherapy dose is high enough to damage cancer cells, but is aimed carefully to minimise harm to healthy tissue. The ALARA principle guides all decisions about radiation exposure in medical, industrial, and research settings. This is a live example of how science informs decisions under uncertainty — evidence about risk at low doses is still being gathered and debated.
exam_tip_html: Questions about the EM spectrum often ask you to “compare” two types of wave — always include wavelength, frequency, energy, and specific uses or dangers. For risk questions, use the phrase “the evidence suggests” rather than stating absolute certainty, especially for low-dose ionising radiation. When asked about the ALARA principle, link it to the idea of making decisions under uncertainty rather than waiting for perfect evidence. A common error is saying X-rays are more dangerous than gamma rays — gamma rays have higher frequency, more energy, and are more penetrating.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All EM waves travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, are transverse, and transfer energy without a medium. They are ordered: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma — increasing frequency and energy.
  • Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays) can remove electrons from atoms and damage DNA, increasing cancer risk. Non-ionising radiation (radio to visible light) carries lower risk but can still harm tissue through heating at high intensity.
  • Every use of ionising radiation in medicine involves a risk-benefit decision. The ALARA principle requires keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable while still obtaining the medical or scientific benefit.

practice_questions.text: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: all travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum; all are transverse waves; all transfer energy; all can travel through a vacuum (do not need a medium) — 1 mark each. Mastering: two distinct properties correctly stated. Secure: two properties. Developing: one correct property. Emerging: vague or incorrect statement.

practice_questions.text: A patient needs a chest X-ray. Explain one benefit and one risk of using X-rays for this medical purpose, and describe how the risk is managed using the ALARA principle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefit — X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and dense structures, enabling diagnosis of fractures, infections, or tumours (2); risk — X-rays are ionising radiation that can damage DNA and potentially cause cancer (2); ALARA — the dose is kept to the minimum needed for a clear image; staff use lead shielding and limit frequency of exposure; benefit of diagnosis outweighs small risk of a single X-ray (2). Secure: 4–5 marks. Developing: 2–3 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves, referring to ionisation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: gamma rays have a much higher frequency (and shorter wavelength) than radio waves (1); higher frequency means more energy per wave — enough to remove electrons from atoms (ionise them) (1); ionisation can damage DNA in cells, potentially causing mutations or cancer; radio waves do not have enough energy to ionise and are considered non-ionising (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how ultraviolet radiation is both useful and potentially harmful. Refer to scientific evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: UV is useful — it causes fluorescence used in security marking and detecting forged banknotes; used in fluorescent lamps; triggers vitamin D production in skin (1+1); UV is harmful — overexposure causes sunburn; repeated overexposure damages DNA in skin cells, increasing risk of skin cancer (1); the evidence linking UV exposure to increased skin cancer rates is well-established from epidemiological studies (1); this illustrates that the same property (energy sufficient to excite electrons) underlies both uses and risks (1). Secure: 3–4 marks. Developing: 2 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties and uses of X-rays and infrared radiation. Include wavelength, frequency, and one use of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: X-rays have shorter wavelength and higher frequency than infrared (1); X-rays are ionising — used in medical imaging to show bones (1); infrared has longer wavelength and lower frequency; it is non-ionising (1); infrared is used in remote controls, thermal imaging, or optical fibre communication (1). Secure: all four points. Developing: three points. Emerging: two points.

practice_questions.text: Describe an investigation a student could carry out to compare the rate of infrared emission from surfaces with different colours and textures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: use a Leslie cube (or beakers with differently coloured surfaces: matt black, shiny silver) filled with hot water (1); place an infrared detector at a fixed, equal distance from each surface (1); record the infrared reading for each surface under identical conditions (same water temperature, same distance) (1); compare results — matt black surface should emit most infrared (1). Secure: all four stages. Developing: three stages. Emerging: two stages.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an ionising type of electromagnetic radiation?
What is the speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?
The EM spectrum in order of increasing frequency begins: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, _____.
Ionising radiation is dangerous because it can damage _____ in cells, potentially causing cancer.
Match each EM wave type to one of its uses.

flashcard_questions.q: What speed do all electromagnetic waves travel at in a vacuum?
List the seven types of EM wave in order of increasing frequency.
flashcard_questions.a: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, UV, X-rays, gamma rays.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions that can damage DNA.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three types of ionising EM radiation.

flashcard_questions.a: As Low As Reasonably Achievable — keep radiation exposure to the lowest practical level.

flashcard_questions.q: What property of X-rays makes them useful for medical imaging?
flashcard_questions.a: They pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and dense materials.

flashcard_questions.q: What does overexposure to UV radiation increase the risk of?
flashcard_questions.a: Skin cancer, by damaging DNA in skin cells.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a microwave oven heat food?
flashcard_questions.a: Microwaves cause water molecules in the food to vibrate, generating heat.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a gamma ray used for in medicine?
flashcard_questions.a: Radiotherapy — targeting and killing cancer cells.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do high-frequency EM waves carry more danger than low-frequency ones?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher frequency means more energy per photon — enough to ionise atoms and damage DNA.

flashcard_questions.q: Are radio waves ionising or non-ionising?
flashcard_questions.a: Non-ionising — they do not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms.

flashcard_questions.q: What is infrared radiation used for in everyday life?
flashcard_questions.a: Remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, and optical fibre communication.

glossary_terms.definition: The continuous family of electromagnetic waves ordered by wavelength or frequency, all sharing the same speed in a vacuum.
EM waves with the longest wavelength and lowest frequency; used for broadcasting radio and television signals and long-range communication.
EM waves between radio and infrared; used in satellite communication, mobile phone networks, and microwave ovens.
EM radiation emitted by all warm objects as heat energy; used in remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, and optical fibre communication.
The narrow part of the EM spectrum detectable by human eyes, ranging from red (longest wavelength) to violet (shortest).
EM radiation with higher frequency than visible light; causes sunburn and increases skin cancer risk; used in fluorescent lamps and security marking.
High-energy EM radiation that passes through soft tissue but is absorbed by bone and dense materials; used in medical imaging; ionising.
The highest-frequency, highest-energy EM waves, emitted by radioactive nuclei; used in radiotherapy and sterilisation; highly ionising.
Electromagnetic radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions; includes UV, X-rays, and gamma rays; can damage DNA and cause cancer.
Electromagnetic radiation that does not have enough energy to ionise atoms; includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, and visible light; generally considered lower risk.
As Low As Reasonably Achievable — the principle that radiation exposure should be minimised to the lowest level practically possible while still achieving the required benefit.
